title: Making air-dried ham at home
subtitle: A dry-cured whole leg hung in moving air over several months. The process is straightforward; the patience is the hard part.
excerpt: Air-dried ham is a whole pig leg packed in curing salt, cold-stored for 3-4 weeks to draw out moisture, then hung in a cool ventilated space for 3-9 months to develop flavour. The result is raw-cured and sliced thin. It requires no smoking, no cooking equipment, and no specialist kit beyond a curing salt and a way to hang the leg.
sourceNotes: Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), home curing chapter. River Cottage Handbook No.13, Curing and Smoking (2011), Chapter on whole hams (reference, copyright-bound). USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, curing meat at home guidance. Traditional curing salt ratios from multiple public-domain American extension service documents.

glossaryTerms.definition: A mixture of table salt and sodium nitrite (and sometimes sodium nitrate) used to preserve meat. Pink in colour. Nitrite inhibits botulism growth and gives cured meat its characteristic colour and flavour. Not to be confused with Himalayan pink salt.
A measure of available water in a food product. Dry-curing reduces water activity below 0.85, a threshold below which most pathogens cannot grow.

projectSchedule.title: Rub and pack in salt
projectSchedule.body: Rub the leg with cure mix, pack in curing salt in a non-reactive container, refrigerate.

projectSchedule.title: Redistribute salt
projectSchedule.body: Turn the leg and redistribute the brine that has formed. Check cure penetration on the thickest part near the bone.

projectSchedule.title: Equalisation period check
projectSchedule.body: Remove from salt, rinse, and pat dry. Begin equalisation at cool temperature before hanging.

projectSchedule.title: Hang to dry
projectSchedule.body: Hang the leg in a cool ventilated space between 10 and 15 degrees C. Monitor for mould weekly.

projectSchedule.title: First taste check
projectSchedule.body: Slice a thin sliver from the exposed face. Check texture and salt level. Decide if it needs more hang time.

content.text: A dry-cured whole ham is one of the most straightforward preserves you can make from a home-grown pig, given a cool space and enough patience. The cure draws moisture out of the meat and
water activity
drops below the threshold where pathogens survive. After that, time does the rest: enzymes break down proteins slowly, flavour compounds accumulate, and the resulting ham slices thin and sweet.
The leg

Start with a leg from a pig slaughtered at 80-100 kg liveweight. A heavier pig gives a leg with enough intramuscular fat to develop flavour during the long hang. Have the abattoir remove the trotter but leave the shank and the skin on, skin protects the surface during the cure and the hang. Weight before curing: typically 7-10 kg for a back leg.
The cure mix
Use a proper
curing salt

from a charcuterie supplier, not plain salt. For a whole air-dried ham using a combination cure: mix 30 g curing salt No. 2 (which contains both nitrite and nitrate for a long cure) with 400 g sea salt, 20 g raw sugar, and 5 g black pepper per kilogram of meat. A 9 kg leg needs approximately 370 g of this mix.
The cure
Pat the leg dry with a clean cloth. Rub the entire surface with the cure mix, including into the shank joint and around the bone at the cut face.
Place in a large non-reactive container (food-grade plastic box or ceramic crock). Pour any remaining cure over the top. Cover and refrigerate at 3-5°C.
After 7 days, turn the leg and redistribute the brine that has formed.
Continue curing for a total of 2-3 days per kilogram of meat weight. A 9 kg leg needs 18-27 days.
Equalisation and hanging
Remove from the brine, rinse under cold water, pat completely dry.
Allow the leg to equalise at fridge temperature for a further week, unwrapped on a rack, before hanging. This lets the salt distribute evenly through the meat.
Hang by the shank in a cool space with moving air, 10-15°C. A garage, cellar, or cool outbuilding in autumn and winter is ideal.

Check weekly. White and grey powdery moulds on the surface are normal and can be wiped with a cloth dipped in white wine vinegar. Green or black mould is a problem: wipe immediately with vinegar and check that the air is moving and humidity is not above 75%.
When is it ready?

Minimum hang time for a home-scale ham is 3 months. Better flavour develops at 6 months; exceptional flavour at 9-12 months. Slice a thin piece from the bone-face of the leg to taste. The meat should be deep red, firm, and slice cleanly. If it is still soft and slightly damp, hang for another month and check again.
